added_claim_errors: Step 2 "budget to spend roughly $1,240+" uses the 2025 $660 cap. For a 2026 plan year with a $680 cap, the required spend is $1,220 (minor, errs on the conservative side).
"about $1,220–$1,240 still forfeits": the range mixes the 2025 and 2026 caps. Only $1,220 is right for 2026 (minor).
Grace period "through March 15" is stated as fixed. March 15 is the legal maximum, and a plan may set a shorter period.
Run-out "often ~90 days after year-end" is an unverified typical figure, though it is hedged and plausible (judged from own knowledge).
"at most $660 of 2025 funds can move into 2026" uses the wrong plan year. The person's plan year ends Dec 31, 2026, and the 2026 cap is $680. B's own Proskauer link gives the 2026 limits.

"you can incur expenses through March 15, 2026 and still claim them against 2025 funds" has the wrong year: for this plan year the latest grace end is March 15, 2027. It also presents March 15 as fixed, when that is only the maximum.

"at most $660 of your $1,900 survives... The March dental work does not get to spend the other $1,240" has the wrong cap and arithmetic for 2026 ($680 and $1,220). It also contradicts the grace-period branch, under which the whole $1,900 can pay for March work done by the grace end.
The suggested HR question "does it run through March 15, 2026?" names the wrong year, which would confuse the check the person needs to make.

reasons: Both answers correct the rollover premise at the start. Both say a plan has one exception or neither, never both. Both send the person to HR about the run-out deadline, warn against prepaying in December for March work, and list eligible items. A gives the correct 2026 carryover cap ($680) and the $1,220 forfeiture figure, though it slips to $1,240 in one step and treats March 15 as a fixed grace end. B is anchored in the wrong plan year throughout: a $660 cap for '2025 funds' and a grace period to March 15, 2026. It also says the March dental work cannot use the other $1,240, which contradicts the grace-period branch. Neither answer properly uses the 2027 open-enrollment election to cover the March work, though A at least mentions next year's election. B is more concise, but its date and cap errors make A clearly better.
